title: Martha confesses Christ and Mary anoints his feet
english: So our Lord did the same when he was about to raise Lazarus from Hades. The compassionate one wept and was moved to his depths as he watched our mortal humanity wasting away, and he grieved together with the crowd that had gathered. Unseen he rebuked death that held Lazarus fast, and visibly he called to the one who was held, and so he worked the great sign of his own power. In it he set before our eyes the pledge of the universal resurrection. That is why he gladly reclined at table with the man he had made, proving by his deeds that he himself is our life and our resurrection. For he had already proclaimed this through the prophet: "I will rejoice in doing them good."

At this marvel and at their own feast, the honored women who learned from the Savior, the sisters of the risen man, served him, one bringing the gifts of welcome and the other the gifts of love for God. For Martha was hospitable like Abraham, generous to the poor like Job, and devoted to Christ in her confession like Peter, and she kept the loving door of welcome open to everyone who came. So she did not entertain angels by surprise and without knowing it, as Lot once did. With full knowledge and a ready heart she received under her roof the maker and Lord of angels. Such was Martha, so great and proven in such great things.

Her sister Mary then, as John the Evangelist says, "took a pound of very costly genuine nard ointment and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment" (John 12:3). The holy women breathed the ointment of devotion and filled the house with the sweet scent of ointment, Martha by her confession and Mary by her deed. Martha is a second Peter. Grace breathed upon her too, and so she poured forth the faith of the chief apostle.

She had heard Jesus say, "Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live" (John 11:25). She recognized the giver of life, and with a sure and piercing voice she cried out, "I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God who comes into the world" (John 11:27). It was necessary for womankind to know and confess the Creator and God. First Peter confesses as taught by God, then Martha cries out as initiated by God, then John theologizes in his writings with a godly mind in the manner of the Only-begotten. Peter and Martha say together, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16). And John says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14).

Mark this, dear reader, the illumination of the truth, and flee the darkness of error. "You are," it says, "the Christ"—not a mere human Christ, but the Son of the living God, the Word become flesh unchanged for us, the only Son of the living God, the Word become flesh. He is not one of the Jewish anointed figures, not one of the Jewish and counterfeit anointed figures. In the words of Paul, you are "the one Lord, blessed over all for ages of ages, amen." You alone are Christ and only-begotten Son of the living God. As the Evangelist says, "We beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14).

You are the firstborn and the only-begotten, and alone with the Holy Spirit you are consubstantial and equally honored and equally mighty with the one who begot you, without beginning and coeternal with God the Father. You are the Christ, not one of the unseen ministering powers you created, but Son of the living God by nature. For, as Isaiah said, "No envoy and no angel, but the Lord himself saved us, he saved them" (Isaiah 63:9). So angels are not christs. You are the Christ, which means not a human Christ but a divine Christ, God incarnate, not a man made divine, but one who, having anointed his own willing becoming flesh with his own divinity, is rightly addressed, "Your name is ointment poured out," and "we will run after the fragrance of your ointments" (Song of Songs 1:3–4). You are the Christ whom all creation worships as one Lord and God, as one Son, as one Master with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Let us turn our speech back again to that most beautiful fellowship of siblings, the devout and faithful brother and sisters. What harmony among the friends and true servants of Christ Jesus, one of the uncreated and consubstantial Trinity.

orientation: The preacher has shown Lazarus at table as proof of a real resurrection and now presents Martha and Mary in confession and love of God.

title: The siblings' faith and Mary's anointing of the living temple
english: What an unbreakable cord is the love of these three! Nothing tore them away from love for their Teacher and Master: not the unbelief of the Jews, not the disobedience of the Pharisees, not the barking of the Sadducees, not the stumbling blocks of the priests. Grafted once into the cultivated olive tree by faith, they remained fruitful, unshaken and unmoved by every assault. They knew Christ as God. They confessed the Son of God as God and man without division and without confusion. They proclaimed Emmanuel. And then Martha said to him, “I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God” (John 11:27). Lazarus confirmed this within himself, having been buried with this faith and hope. For while he was still alive and joining in supplication to the one present everywhere, his sisters pleaded on his behalf, saying, “Lord, see, the one you love is ill” (John 11:3). And Mary, through what she did, displayed her own piety in harmony with her sister’s confession and her brother’s faith.

Taking the ointment, she did not anoint a lifeless stone as a house of God, as Jacob did for the one who appeared to him when he was fleeing Esau. Rather, she anointed the living temple united from the God-bearing virgin to the uncreated God and Maker of all things. She was not merely preserving a likeness of the kinship with Jacob in these things, as a true daughter, but far surpassing the patriarch in faith and deed. For he was sketching the shadow, while she was touching and worshiping the truth itself.

Jacob appears to have done this twice: once when he was fleeing the envy armed for murder, and once when he returned after the divine vision at Bethel. But even so he is not made equal to his daughter’s piety in this matter. For he learned nothing more than to anoint a stone as a type of the cornerstone, while she not only touched and anointed the holy, living, God-built temple of the uncreated and eternal God, but also worshiped the God who is in it without division, together with it and through it. Confessing one Lord without division, she perceived the invisible glory in the visible beauty, and in the flesh that could be touched she discerned the untouchable and intangible God the Word.

For his conforming himself to us did not diminish the glory of the invisible God in their eyes. The lowliness of his reclining at table with them did not insult the magnificent authority of God in their eyes. The weak garment of flesh did not reduce the judgment of their minds concerning his unapproachable supremacy. The boldness of their love toward his condescension did not blunt the fear and trembling before his unbearable power. Rather, guided from the visible signs to the invisible might, they marveled exceedingly at the paradox of his voluntary poverty. Illumined in mind by the wonders beyond reason that were accomplished by his words, and instructed in the authoritative power of his lordship, they shuddered all the more at his loving incarnation. Seeing the outpouring of healings bestowed through the touch of the hem, they worshiped the God who works without hindrance and pours out help from his own treasury. And contemplating the resurrection of the dead, they were utterly astonished at death's dwelling among mortals.

Therefore, mingling fear with affection, they held fast to an insatiable longing. The sisters, of one soul and one faith, divided between themselves the service of the one and the same Lord, who is God and perfect man in union. Martha ministered to his human needs because of his condescension toward us, while Mary offered a devotion pleasing to God and most fragrant as a first-fruits offering, pouring ointment on his life-giving temple as upon an altar. And this she did not carelessly but with diligence, kissing it and wiping the holy thing with her natural covering. She placed a crown of glory on her own head, not one composed of corruptible and earthly material, but one flashing with the radiance of divine splendor.

If, then, according to Moses, “everyone who touches the altar shall be sanctified” (Exodus 29:37 LXX), what could anyone say about the woman who touched the Lord of the altar himself? With what words shall we adorn the harmony of these siblings? Yes, their works surpass all praise. Martha, your confession of Christ is enough for a crown of glory. Lazarus, being called the friend of Christ is enough for an abundance of glory. Mary, the verdict from God is enough for you.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG 18 Homilia christologica in Lazarum u02-rem-mid
orientation: The preacher is praising the three siblings of Bethany, showing how their faith, confession, and Mary's anointing of Jesus surpass the old types such as Jacob's anointing of the stone.

title: Mary's quiet contemplation, the blind Jew's objection, and the doxology
english: For Mary, he says, “has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). Mary the lover of quiet, the solitary bee, who hovers over the meadows of divine contemplation, who became a sojourner and exile from the muddied life and arrived at the untroubled divine life that befits the peaceful. “Where there is a gentle breeze, there also is the Lord” (1 Kings 19:12), according to the oracle of Elijah; from this springs knowledge of divine and human matters, as it is written, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10 LXX). She is the pure dove, who gently lifted her wings and came to rest in the calm and blessed harbor of stillness, through which she was initiated into the things longed for by prophets and righteous people. Jacob fled from a turbulent spear and, at an opportune time encountered God, and anointed a pillar of remembrance, as has often been said; and Mary, having separated herself far from the rush of mixed and motley thoughts that somehow roughen the most transparent cell of thought and mind, untroubled herself, heard the blessings of God, and was counted worthy to grasp the ungraspable one through flesh.

But the Jew in his blindness leaps upon the argument and says: Do not blaspheme, Christian, for it is written, “No one shall see my face and live, says the Lord” (Exodus 33:20). Indeed, you fool, in your own law it is written that Jacob said, “I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved” (Genesis 32:30); for the vision of God is life for a human being. And since these things stand so, I will neither nullify your text nor leave my own word without witness. For it is impossible and beyond all means to comprehend the substance of God, yet it is easy for God to be made known to human beings, since he who is all-powerful reveals himself to the worthy as he wills. For it is written, “I multiplied visions, and in the hands of the prophets I was likened” (Hosea 12:10).

Jacob, then, saw God, and did not lie; but he saw him as the one who appeared willed to be seen. For God knows how to reveal himself as he wills, and there is nothing that hinders or blocks his purpose, even if not even the highest powers can bear his glory to the utmost. So also Mary saw God incarnate without change, and upon his holy and co-worshipped temple she poured a libation of fragrance—that is, upon himself, for the union is without division, and the mystery of piety is without confusion, and the confession of the one of the Trinity, the Lord Jesus Christ, is without division.

But you, beloved, do not be surprised when you hear something strange and discordant from those who are strangers to the truth. For they are brothers of the blind traitor Judas, who foolishly criticized this God-pleasing purpose at the supper. But what did the incorruptible verdict say to him? It convicts Judas as a thief, and receives her as a lover of God, and proclaims what was done as a good work, and stands against those who bring charges. And he says these things through Matthew the evangelist: “Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a good work for me” (Matthew 26:10). And I weigh against the love of such a work the eternal remembrance: “For wherever this gospel of the kingdom is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be spoken in memory of her” (Matthew 26:13).

And worthy of the sowing is the harvest of Mary, and worthy of the good purpose is the fruit. She hastened to fulfill the Scripture; she was anticipated by the divine grace that crowns her. She learned the things sung in the prophets; she recognized the timely fulfillment of the prophecy. She heard Solomon singing, “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song of Solomon 1:12), and she understood the King of kings and Lord of lords foretold by the servant king. Therefore, without delaying at all, she completed the work of her learning, and bringing to the one who lacks nothing what had been foretold, she carried away the glorious and undeceiving verdict. With which may it be granted that all of us, knowing and worshipping one and the same Lord, begotten before the ages co-eternally and equally without beginning, ineffably and without emanation, from the Father—that is, from the uncreated substance—and in the last days from the undefiled Virgin, without change and without confusion, beyond thought and word, made flesh, may obtain the blessing that comes from him, in mercy and endless life. For to him be glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to the ageless ages of ages. Amen.
